Neonatal meerkats emerge from the natal burrow at about three weeks of age, but the transition to nutritional independence is a gradual process. The time since birth at weaning has been documented at 44 days [tx = 44 days] under captive conditions at the species' typical core body temperature of 36.3 °C [T = 36.3 °C]. At this juncture, the pups have achieved a wet weight at weaning of 225.5 grams [Wwx = 225.5 grams], a nearly eightfold increase from their birth mass. This substantial gain reflects the high energetic subsidy provided by the colony's lactating females and the protein-rich invertebrate prey that begins to supplement the milk diet. The weaning process in this cooperative breeder is notably synchronous across a litter, with all pups typically reaching this milestone within a narrow timeframe. The early provisioning by helpers, including non-breeding adults and sub-adults, is critical for ensuring that the pups attain this weaning weight, which is necessary for them to begin foraging independently alongside the group.

In contrast to the altricial state of many small carnivores, the meerkat neonate is born with closed eyes and scant fur, weighing a mere 29 grams [Wwb = 29 grams] at delivery. This low birth mass places the pups in a highly vulnerable position, dependent entirely on the thermal and nutritional care of the colony. The ultimate wet weight, the maximum body mass recorded for an adult meerkat, is approximately 776 grams [Wwi = approximately 776 grams] for a robust, dominant individual. This represents a substantial size dimorphism compared to the neonatal stage, with adults having achieved a 26-fold increase in mass. The rapid growth trajectory is fueled by a diet almost exclusively composed of arthropods, with scorpions and beetles forming a major component. The ability of subordinate females to also lactate and provision pups is a hallmark of their cooperative breeding system, ensuring that the nutritional demands of multiple litters can be met simultaneously within the social group.

At the species' typical active body temperature of 36.3 °C [T = 36.3 °C], the reproductive output of the dominant female is a key driver of population dynamics. Field records indicate that she can produce up to four pups per litter [N_R_i = up to four pups per litter], a relatively large litter size for a mammal of this body size. Under favorable conditions, she may initiate multiple reproductive cycles within a single season, typically achieving a maximum of one litter per year [F_R_i = one litter per year]. The gestation time, from successful copulation to parturition, lasts for 77 days [tg = 77 days] at the standard thermoneutral body temperature at a temperature of 36.3 °C [T = 36.3 °C]. This relatively short gestation for a mammal of this size is followed by an extended period of post-natal dependency. The timing of these litters is tightly linked to seasonal rainfall patterns, which drive the abundance of their insect prey. The high energetic cost of gestation is borne almost entirely by the dominant female, though the entire colony shares in the subsequent care of the resultant litter.

Puberty, or the onset of sexual maturation, does not happen immediately upon reaching adult body size. For a female meerkat, the time since birth at puberty is typically around 365 days [tp = around 365 days], occurring at a core body temperature of 36.3 °C [T = 36.3 °C]. This milestone marks the point at which a female is physiologically capable of reproducing, but social suppression by the dominant breeding pair often prevents subordinates from doing so. This reproductive suppression is mediated through aggressive behavior and hormonal cues, effectively limiting breeding to the alpha pair. The age at first reproduction is therefore often significantly later than the age at puberty for females that remain in their natal group. Dispersal to a new territory, often following the death of a dominant individual, is a common prerequisite for a subordinate female to achieve breeding status and successfully produce her first litter.

Among the small carnivores of the family Herpestidae, the maximum recorded lifespan for a wild meerkat has been estimated at 20.6 years [am = 20.6 years] at the species' typical active body temperature of 36.3 °C [T = 36.3 °C], though this value is likely only attainable under favorable conditions with minimal predation and disease pressure. This longevity is surprisingly high for a mammal of its modest mass — Suricata suricatta is one of the longer-lived herpestids documented. Such an extended lifespan is unusual among similarly sized carnivores and is thought to be linked to their cooperative social structure, which reduces individual predation risk and buffers against food shortages. The presence of a stable group of helpers allows older, senescent individuals to survive periods of resource scarcity. Ultimately, natural death in meerkats is often the result of a combination of factors including predation by raptors and snakes, disease, and intraspecific conflict with neighboring groups, which can be particularly violent and lead to significant mortality among both pups and adults.
